Research

We build systems that explore rather than reproduce. Duetto is where that question meets the human body — a real-time dialogue between a dancer and a generative model.

Why movement

Foundations

Building a system designed for genuine exploration means the choice of domain is not neutral. We chose the human body because it sits in a uniquely productive position: concrete enough to measure, open-ended enough to be genuinely creative.

Human movement is the expression of a complex dynamical system — a high-dimensional trajectory through phase space, non-stationary, sensitive to initial conditions, continuously modulated by the feedback between internal state and external environment. As a time series it carries information across simultaneous timescales, from joint-level dynamics to gestural phrasing, and stays entangled with intention and context in ways that make it irreducible to pure biomechanics.

A spectrum of semantic constraint

Unlike language, where a misplaced word breaks coherence, movement operates across a range of tolerances. Expressive domains such as dance afford vast combinatorial freedom: the syntax is permissive and novelty is not an error. Procedural domains — a surgeon operating, an athlete executing a technique — impose tight boundaries where deviation carries real cost.

The same body, the same joints, the same physics, but an entirely different tolerance for variation. That spectrum is a feature: it means a movement model is not one fixed notion of correctness, but a framework that calibrates its generative logic to the semantic regime of the application.

The Large Movement Model

Model

What made large language models possible was not scale alone, but the insight that language has a grammar: an underlying statistical structure that, learned deeply enough, allows a system to generate coherent and even creative output.

Movement has a grammar too. A Large Movement Model is to the body what a language model is to language — joints serve as vocabulary, movement sequences as sentences, and the model learns the underlying rules of how a body moves through space and time.

Duetto

Application

Duetto is the first application and proof of concept of the Large Movement Model, built around two questions: how technology can enrich dancers’ creative practices, and whether deep learning can power a movement suggestion system for dancers.

The core challenge is a generative system capable of continuous, real-time, bidirectional interaction with a human performer — without the latency that would break creative flow. To the best of current knowledge this remains an open problem in the field. The human moves, the system listens, the system proposes, the human responds.

Why dance

Dance was chosen not because it is the only application, but because it represents the upper bound of movement complexity: maximally free, expressive, and creative. If a system can hold a dialogue with a dancer, it can hold one with any body in any context.

How it works

Method

The pipeline starts from video, from which we extract audio signals, high-dimensional motion capture, and multimodal input from the body in movement. From there the model learns to compress and structure that data into latent representations, then to generate new movement rather than memorise what it has seen.

Data collection

In the first session we recruited dancers across three experience levels — professional, semi-professional, non-professional — and captured their movement across nine musical conditions varying in intensity, style, and tempo, to maximise diversity in the training distribution.

In the second session, sixteen professional dancers each performed four improvised pieces under choreographic guidance. In two of the four trials they moved while viewing a skeletonised projection of their own body — a feedback condition that directly informed the design of the interactive system.

Pose estimation

Movement is captured with sVision, our real-time human pose estimation pipeline, which extracts key anatomical landmarks and represents the body as a set of spatial coordinates evolving over time.

Quantising the body

Raw joint coordinates must be transformed into a discrete vocabulary a generative model can process. The choice of quantisation framework determines whether the resulting token space is interpretable and controllable, or simply a black box.

VQ-VAE is the current state of the art and serves as our baseline. Building on it we developed SOM-VQ, which combines vector quantisation with Self-Organising Maps to give the codebook an explicit spatial structure: tokens that are close together represent similar postures. This turns the codebook into a navigable map of movement, and that structure is what makes real human-in-the-loop interaction possible — a dancer can steer the system by moving through the map, diverging from a reference, exploring nearby regions, or returning toward a target. Control is not an add-on; it grows out of how the space is organised.

The generative model

Built on top of the quantised representation, the generative core is an autoregressive model that produces movement token by token, conditioning each output on both the history of past states and the live input from the performer.

The critical requirement is real-time generation: the system must produce new movement at every step, not replay cached sequences, and fast enough to sustain unbroken interaction.

Divergence as dialogue

The spatial gap between where the machine is and where the performer is, is not an error — it is the creative distance the system navigates. Proximity is enforced by the topology of the map rather than by rules, continuously re-anchoring generation toward the human.

Staying open

Theory

Generative models are remarkably good at compressing and reproducing the world, but every time they do they risk losing part of their diversity. Trained recursively on their own synthetic output, they progressively lose diversity and degrade — what is now called model collapse.

We found the problem runs deeper than architecture or scale. When a model is trained on a finite set of examples through repeated resampling, collapse eventually becomes inevitable. We identified the iteration at which some of the original diversity disappears irreversibly, and call it the extinction threshold.

Recursion as the cure

The problem is not recursion in itself — it is passive recursion. Dreaming Learning uses the model’s own synthetic output during training, but to generate trajectories that maximise exploration while remaining anchored to the real distribution. Synthetic data becomes a controlled exploratory mechanism rather than a cheap substitute for real data.

Alongside it, Lyapunov Learning at the Onset of Chaos trains models to operate between rigidity and noise — the regime where a system is both sensitive and structured.

Why this matters for a dancer

A system that learns only from one person risks becoming a mirror: increasingly faithful, increasingly useless. This is model collapse at a personal scale — not the loss of diversity across a population, but the loss of the capacity to surprise. Dreaming Learning is the mechanism that lets the system know a body deeply and, from that knowledge, still offer a movement it has never tried.

Beyond the stage

Outlook

Everything built for the dancer applies to any body in motion: a gym, a rehabilitation studio, a training field. A system that observes not how an ideal athlete moves, nor how a statistical average moves, but how you move — your habits, your asymmetries, your recurring patterns — and keeps learning session after session.

The architecture built for dance is not a dance architecture. It is an architecture for any body, in any domain, with any tolerance for variation: the same logic, calibrated differently.

Live performances

Live

Duetto made its first public appearance at the IntelligentIA event through two live performances designed as a progressive experiment.

The first started in fully synchronous mode, the digital skeleton mirroring the dancer in real time, before a temporal delay was gradually introduced and a visible misalignment opened between the two bodies. The second shifted from synchrony into full generative mode, where the skeleton began to propose movement rather than follow it.

Together they mapped the project’s research trajectory — from imitation to interaction — functioning at once as artistic statement and as experimental demonstration of the system’s capacity to move between operational modes.
